_doc: Carriage modes. crew_trade: the trade whose hours drive the carrier (the labour package counts them as carriage need). edge_classes: land, river, coast, open_sea. requires_nodes: tech nodes a party must hold to use the mode. needs_improvement: key the caller's improvements dict must carry on the edge (built roads and track). model picks the physics in sim/geography/routes_rates.py and carrier holds its inputs. critical_grade: grade at which pace halves. max_grade: grade above which the mode cannot be used. built_grade_cap: grade a built improvement is levelled to; max_natural_grade: steepest natural grade it can be built over without an 'engineered' improvement. km_factor: share of the edge's km a built way keeps. engineered: {max_grade, earthwork_factor, kind, conf, source, why} lets a built way cross ground steeper than max_natural_grade up to max_grade, with the cut-and-fill bench multiplied by earthwork_factor (cuttings, embankments, retaining walls); the caller records the edge as engineered. river_crossing: how a land mode meets a river crossing (a land edge between tiles on the same river): absent means the carrier fords or ferries it, paying the mode's own handling once; "bridge_only" means it cannot cross without a built bridge; "none" means the mode's works carry their own crossings. handling_hours_per_tonne and handling_days: load and unload each time a haul changes to this mode. dues_hours_per_tonne (with dues_conf and dues_source): tolls or port dues charged on the same occasion; absent means none.

entries.label: Porters on foot
entries.source: Research notes section 3: porters carry 25 to 30 kg at 20 to 25 km a day.
entries.why: Carriage with no animal and no road, available on any land edge.

entries.label: Pack animals
entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: road, bridge and gate tolls, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.source: sim/geography/transport.py pack_freight_physical_inputs; grade limits from research notes section 2.
entries.why: Caravans and mule strings cross rough country without a road.

entries.label: Carts on a track
entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: road, bridge and gate tolls, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.source: sim/geography/transport.py draught_freight_physical_inputs; wheeled critical slopes from research notes section 2.
entries.why: Wheeled carriage on the unbuilt track between tiles; mountains stop it.

entries.label: Carts on a built road

engineered.source: Labelled heuristic: a cutting or embankment through ground steeper than the natural limit moves a multiple of the side-hill bench, with retaining walls and rock work. Not fitted to a source.
engineered.why: Lets a road be carried over steep ground at a higher earthwork cost.

construction.source: Labelled heuristic: the crew is the labourers one project can work at once and the working days a year are a round figure, so the build time is the person-days over the crew's days in a year; a metalled road a cart can use is a few metres of carriageway on a levelled bed with a stone surface; hand excavation of a few cubic metres a person-day is the order of ancient earthwork rates. Not fitted to a source.
construction.why: What building a road costs per km from its width, bed and surface; the relief adds a cut-and-fill bench (see sim/geography/ways_build.py).

entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: road, bridge and gate tolls, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.source: sim/geography/transport.py PAVED_ROAD; Roman road grades of 4 to 12 percent and circuity 1.1 to 1.2 from research notes sections 2 and 5.
entries.why: A built road lowers rolling resistance, is levelled to a gentler grade and runs straighter than a track.

entries.label: Steam railway

engineered.source: Labelled heuristic: a cutting or embankment through ground steeper than the natural limit moves a multiple of the side-hill bench, with retaining walls and rock work. Not fitted to a source.
engineered.why: Lets a railway be carried over steep ground at a higher earthwork cost.

construction.source: Labelled heuristic: the crew is the labourers one project can work at once and the working days a year are a round figure, so the build time is the person-days over the crew's days in a year; two iron edge rails of a few tens of kilograms a metre on a ballasted bed. Not fitted to a source.
construction.why: What laying a railway costs per km from its bed, ballast and rails; the relief adds a cut-and-fill bench (see sim/geography/ways_build.py).

entries.source: Research notes sections 3 and 5: early steam trains at 30 to 40 km/h, ruling grades of 1 to 1.5 percent, steel-on-steel rolling resistance 0.1 to 0.2 percent; engine efficiency of a few percent. The rolling stock (a mass of locomotive and wagons per tonne of cargo, in iron, and a service life in kilometres) is a labelled heuristic that prices the train as a freight carrier (sim/geography/rail_freight.py).
entries.why: Needs built track; the ruling grade bounds the line, so steeper natural ground needs earthwork.

entries.label: River boats
entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: river tolls at bridges, weirs and lock or staithe stations, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.why: Towed barges; the current speeds the way down and slows the way up.

entries.label: Barges on a canal

engineered.source: Labelled heuristic: a canal over steeper ground is stepped by flights of locks and cut through the rise. Not fitted to a source.
engineered.why: Lets a canal climb ground steeper than the natural limit at a higher earthwork cost.

construction.source: Labelled heuristic: a towpath barge canal of a few metres' depth and a dozen metres' width, cut by hand, with stone revetment and lock gates of timber; the crew and working days are round figures as for a road. Not fitted to a source.
construction.why: What cutting a canal costs per km from its channel and lining; the relief adds a cut-and-fill bench (see sim/geography/ways_build.py).

entries.source: sim/geography/transport.py barge_freight_physical_inputs, towed along the bank on still water.
entries.why: Towed barges on a built channel: still water at the levelled grade, so no current helps or hinders.

entries.label: Sailing ships
entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: harbour, anchorage and quay dues, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.source: sim/geography/sea_freight.py; coast-hugging is slower than open-water sailing per research notes section 6.
entries.why: Wind-driven hulls between ports; both ends of a leg are coastal tiles.

entries.label: Steamships
entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: harbour, anchorage and quay dues, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.source: Research notes section 3: early steamships carry 1 to 3 kt at 250 to 400 km a day, coal heavy on long voyages.
entries.why: Engine-driven hulls ignore the wind and can stem a river current.
